question: What did COA observe about cash advances in Manila?

answer.summary: In its 2021 and 2024 audit reports, COA observed significant balances of unliquidated cash advances in the City of Manila—₱182.725 million in CY 2021 and ₱358.524 million in CY 2024. COA highlighted delays in liquidation, substantial amounts tied to separated or deceased personnel, and the granting of additional cash advances despite unsettled prior balances.

key_points.text: In the CY 2024 audit, COA observed that cash advances totaling ₱358.524 million (or ₱355.158 million per paragraph 2.a) remained unliquidated as of December 31, 2024, due to non-submission of liquidation reports by Accountable Officers (AOs). Of this balance, ₱148.307 million (41.37%) had been outstanding from over 60 days to more than 10 years, making them due and demandable.

This included ₱38.500 million for one deceased AO requested by Management for write-off as a dormant receivable.

question: Did Manila comply with IPSAS 1 in its financial statements? Which years?

answer.summary: COA's Annual Audit Reports show that the City of Manila did not fully comply with IPSAS 1 (Presentation of Financial Statements), particularly its requirement to present fairly the City's financial position, performance, and cash flows. COA specifically cited non-compliance with IPSAS 1 in CY 2020, CY 2022, CY 2023, and CY 2024 across various asset, liability, inventory, and adjustment accounts.

key_points.text: In CY 2020, COA cited IPSAS fair presentation requirements under Observation No. 1, noting that accounting errors in Cash-in-Bank transactions totaling P66.815 million (including unrecorded checks and unadjusted reconciling items) weighed on the fair presentation of accounts in the financial statements.

citations.text: CY 2020 AAR, Part II, Observation No. 1, pp. 69-71
citations.title: Accounting errors in recording cash-in-bank (CiB) transactions amounting to P66.815 million resulted in the misstatement of affected CiB accounts and weighed on the fair presentation of these accounts in the City’s Fg Statements (FS).

key_points.text: In CY 2022, COA found the City non-compliant with Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 under Observation No. 1 because inventory accounts were overstated by a net P32.595 million due to record-keeping deficiencies, lack of required inventory ledgers, and unreconciled records between the accounting and property offices.

citations.text: CY 2022 AAR, Part II, Observation No. 1, pp. 73-76
citations.title: The inventory accounts were overstated by a net amount of P32.595 million due to accounting errors in record keeping, non-maintenance of inventory records and unreconciled records of the Office of the City Accountant (OCAT) and City General Services Office (CGSO) contrary to Paragraph 27 of the International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) 1. This condition weighed on the fairness of the presentation of the inventories in the Financial Statement (FS).

key_points.text: In CY 2023, COA observed non-compliance with Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 under Observation No. 2, finding that the accuracy and reliability of the P4.577 billion Accounts Payable balance could not be determined due to a net understatement variance of P525.085 million against supplier confirmations and the failure to maintain separate subsidiary ledgers for each contractor/supplier.

citations.text: CY 2023 AAR, Part II, Observation No. 2, pp. 75-77
citations.title: The accuracy, completeness, and reliability of the year-end balance of Accounts Payable (AP) amounting to P4.577 billion could not be determined due to net understatement variance of P525.085 million from confirmation results with contractors/suppliers as against balances per books contrary to Paragraph 27 of International Public Sector Accounting Standard (IPSAS) 1. Thus, affecting the fair presentation of the FS.

key_points.text: In CY 2024, COA reported widespread non-compliance with Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 across major financial statement accounts, including Cash-in-Bank (unadjusted reconciling items and bank variances), Receivables (unsupported balances and a P1.207 billion discrepancy in RPT/SET receivables), Accounts Payable (a P608.320 million variance with suppliers), and PPE accounts such as Buildings, Medical Equipment, and Construction in Progress (unreconciled discrepancies in the billions of pesos).

question: Did Manila act on COA's recommendations about cash advances?

answer.summary: Across the 2020 through 2023 Annual Audit Reports, Manila took action on prior audit recommendations concerning cash advances—such as sending demand letters and recording liquidations—leading COA to evaluate previous findings from 2018, 2019, and 2021 as implemented by 2023. However, in the 2024 report, COA observed recurring deficiencies, finding P358.52 million in unliquidated cash advances, long-outstanding balances from separated employees, and newly granted advances to officers with unsettled accounts.

key_points.text: For recommendations raised in the CY 2019 audit, Manila required certification to avoid overlapping advances, leading COA to assess the rule against granting additional advances as fully implemented by 2021. The recommendation to require accountable officers to authorize salary deductions for unliquidated advances was rated not implemented in 2020, partially implemented in 2021 and 2022, and marked implemented in 2023.
